claim: iSBH-sgRNAs enable conditional CRISPR activation in response to RNA detection in HEK293T cells.
source: Here, we present a simple and specific platform for modulating CRISPR activity in response to RNA detection through engineering Streptococcus pyogenes Cas9 single-guide RNAs (sgRNAs).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing CRISPR activation in HEK293T cells using iSBH-sgRNAs in response to RNA triggers, as demonstrated in Figure 1 and related experiments.

claim: iSBH-sgRNAs enable conditional CRISPR activation in response to RNA detection in zebrafish embryos.
source: Our approach enables CRISPR activation in response to RNA detection in both HEK293T cells and zebrafish embryos.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing CRISPR activation in zebrafish embryos using chemically modified iSBH-sgRNAs, as demonstrated in Figure 5.

claim: Engineered sgRNAs are cleaved during RNA detection.
source: Mechanistic investigations reveal that engineered sgRNAs are cleaved during RNA detection, and we identify key positions that benefit from chemical modifications to improve the stability of engineered sgRNAs in vivo.
evidence: RNA circularisation assays demonstrated that iSBH-sgRNAs are truncated during activation, as shown in Figure 4.

claim: Chemical modifications at key positions improve the stability of engineered sgRNAs in vivo.
source: Mechanistic investigations reveal that engineered sgRNAs are cleaved during RNA detection, and we identify key positions that benefit from chemical modifications to improve the stability of engineered sgRNAs in vivo.
evidence: The manuscript shows that chemical modifications protecting the 5' end of the iSBH-sgRNA and the 5' end of the spacer improved function in zebrafish embryos, as demonstrated in Figure 5.

claim: Cellular transcripts encode important information regarding cell identity and disease status.
source: Since cellular RNAs offer crucial information about cell identity, differentiation, disease status, and environmental exposure (Abdolhosseini et al., 2019; Kotliar et al., 2019), modulating CRISPR activation in response to RNA detection holds tremendous promise for future innovations.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The single-guide RNA (sgRNA) component of Streptococcus pyogenes CRISPR-Cas9 systems tolerates extensive modifications.
source: The single-guide RNA (sgRNA) component of Streptococcus pyogenes CRISPR-Cas9 systems (Jinek et al., 2012) tolerates extensive modifications and sgRNA engineering has been established as a method for controlling CRISPR activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Jinek et al., 2012 and is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Inactivated sgRNAs can be re-activated in response to small molecules.
source: Inactivated sgRNAs can be successfully re-activated in response to small molecules (Tang et al., 2017), proteins (Ferry et al., 2017), DNA antisense oligonucleotides (Ferry et al., 2017), as well as RNA (Hanewich-Hollatz et al., 2019; Hochrein et al., 2021; Jakimo et al., 2018; Jiao et al., 2021; Jin et al., 2019; Li et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2022; Lin et al., 2020; Siu and Chen, 2019; Galizi et al., 2020; Hunt and Chen, 2022a; Hunt and Chen, 2022b; Ying et al., 2020; Choi et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Tang et al., 2017.

claim: Inactivated sgRNAs can be re-activated in response to proteins.
source: Inactivated sgRNAs can be successfully re-activated in response to small molecules (Tang et al., 2017), proteins (Ferry et al., 2017), DNA antisense oligonucleotides (Ferry et al., 2017), as well as RNA (Hanewich-Hollatz et al., 2019; Hochrein et al., 2021; Jakimo et al., 2018; Jiao et al., 2021; Jin et al., 2019; Li et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2022; Lin et al., 2020; Siu and Chen, 2019; Galizi et al., 2020; Hunt and Chen, 2022a; Hunt and Chen, 2022b; Ying et al., 2020; Choi et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ferry et al., 2017.

claim: Inactivated sgRNAs can be re-activated in response to DNA antisense oligonucleotides.
source: Inactivated sgRNAs can be successfully re-activated in response to small molecules (Tang et al., 2017), proteins (Ferry et al., 2017), DNA antisense oligonucleotides (Ferry et al., 2017), as well as RNA (Hanewich-Hollatz et al., 2019; Hochrein et al., 2021; Jakimo et al., 2018; Jiao et al., 2021; Jin et al., 2019; Li et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2022; Lin et al., 2020; Siu and Chen, 2019; Galizi et al., 2020; Hunt and Chen, 2022a; Hunt and Chen, 2022b; Ying et al., 2020; Choi et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ferry et al., 2017.

claim: Inactivated sgRNAs can be re-activated in response to RNA.
source: Inactivated sgRNAs can be successfully re-activated in response to small molecules (Tang et al., 2017), proteins (Ferry et al., 2017), DNA antisense oligonucleotides (Ferry et al., 2017), as well as RNA (Hanewich-Hollatz et al., 2019; Hochrein et al., 2021; Jakimo et al., 2018; Jiao et al., 2021; Jin et al., 2019; Li et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2022; Lin et al., 2020; Siu and Chen, 2019; Galizi et al., 2020; Hunt and Chen, 2022a; Hunt and Chen, 2022b; Ying et al., 2020; Choi et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Published technologies that rely on sgRNA engineering require improvement to enhance the dynamic range of activation.
source: While limited evidence is available for the modulation of CRISPR activity following RNA detection in mammalian cells (Hanewich-Hollatz et al., 2019; Hochrein et al., 2021; Hunt and Chen, 2022a; Hunt and Chen, 2022b; Lin et al., 2020; Ying et al., 2020), published technologies that rely on sgRNA engineering still require improvement to enhance the dynamic range of activation.
evidence: This is an assessment of the state of the field based on cited literature.

claim: There is no clear evidence that existing engineering approaches can be generalised to detect a diverse panel of RNA sequences.
source: There is no clear evidence that existing engineering approaches can be generalised to detect a diverse panel of RNA sequences.
evidence: This is an assessment of the state of the field based on literature review.

claim: Functional validation of engineered sgRNAs in vivo remains unexplored.
source: Additionally, functional validation of engineered sgRNAs in vivo remains unexplored.
evidence: This is an assessment of the state of the field based on literature review.

claim: Native sgRNAs have two components: the spacer and scaffold sequences.
source: Native sgRNAs have two components: the spacer and scaffold sequences. The spacer sequence is complementary to the CRISPR-targeting sequence (CTS) and determines sgRNA specificity, while the scaffold sequence stabilises interactions between the sgRNA and Cas9 proteins (Figure 1A, Jinek et al., 2012; Gaj et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The spacer sequence is complementary to the CRISPR-targeting sequence (CTS) and determines sgRNA specificity.
source: The spacer sequence is complementary to the CRISPR-targeting sequence (CTS) and determines sgRNA specificity, while the scaffold sequence stabilises interactions between the sgRNA and Cas9 proteins (Figure 1A, Jinek et al., 2012; Gaj et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The scaffold sequence stabilises interactions between the sgRNA and Cas9 proteins.
source: The spacer sequence is complementary to the CRISPR-targeting sequence (CTS) and determines sgRNA specificity, while the scaffold sequence stabilises interactions between the sgRNA and Cas9 proteins (Figure 1A, Jinek et al., 2012; Gaj et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: iSBH-sgRNA designs differ from native sgRNAs by having a 14-nucleotide loop and a partially complementary spacer* sequence in addition to the spacer and scaffold sequences.
source: They differ from native sgRNAs by having a 14-nucleotide loop and a partially complementary spacer* sequence in addition to the spacer and scaffold sequences.
evidence: This is a description of the design features of iSBH-sgRNAs developed in this study.

claim: The complementarity between the spacer and spacer* sequences creates a complex secondary structure that inactivates the sgRNA function.
source: The complementarity between the spacer and spacer* sequences creates a complex secondary structure that inactivates the sgRNA function (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a description of the mechanism supported by the design and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: When iSBH-sgRNAs are introduced into cells that do not express complementary RNA sequences, spacer sequences are blocked, and CRISPR activity is turned OFF.
source: When iSBH-sgRNAs are introduced into cells that do not express complementary RNA sequences, spacer sequences are blocked, and CRISPR activity is turned OFF.
evidence: This is a description of the expected behavior of the system, supported by experimental data in Figure 1.

claim: When RNA sequences complementary to the loop and spacer* sequences are present, the iSBH-sgRNA conformation changes, exposing spacer sequences and turning ON CRISPR activity.
source: However, when RNA sequences complementary to the loop and spacer* sequences are present, the iSBH-sgRNA conformation changes, exposing spacer sequences and turning ON CRISPR activity.
evidence: This is a description of the expected behavior of the system, supported by experimental data in Figure 1.

claim: iSBH-sgRNAs only become activated in the presence of their corresponding triggers.
source: Data showed that iSBH-sgRNAs only become activated in the presence of their corresponding triggers, suggesting the exquisite activation specificity of our system.
evidence: This is supported by orthogonality test data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Orthogonality between different iSBH-sgRNA and their triggers suggests that multiple iSBH-sgRNA trigger pairs could be incorporated within genetic circuits and used in parallel for performing different tasks.
source: Furthermore, orthogonality between different iSBH-sgRNA and their triggers suggested that multiple iSBH-sgRNA trigger pairs could be incorporated within genetic circuits and used in parallel for performing different tasks.
evidence: This is an inference based on the orthogonality data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Second-generation iSBH-sgRNAs were designed by extending the length of the iSBH-sgRNA backfold complementary with the RNA trigger.
source: Starting from this principle, second-generation iSBH-sgRNAs were designed by extending the length of the iSBH-sgRNA backfold complementary with the RNA trigger.
evidence: This is a description of the design strategy for second-generation iSBH-sgRNAs.

claim: A 10 nucleotide (nt) extension was introduced between the spacer and loop sequences, resulting in a 30 nt backfold.
source: A 10 nucleotide (nt) extension was introduced between the spacer and loop sequences, resulting in a 30 nt backfold.
evidence: This is a description of the design features of second-generation iSBH-sgRNAs.

claim: Increasing the size of iSBH-sgRNAs enabled increasing the size of complementary RNA triggers from 34 to 44 nt.
source: Increasing the size of iSBH-sgRNAs enabled increasing the size of complementary RNA triggers from 34 to 44 nt (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a description of the design features supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: dCas9-Vp64 and 8xCTS-ECFP had the cleanest OFF-state for second-generation iSBH-sgRNA designs.
source: In concordance with our observations for first-generation iSBH-sgRNA designs, dCas9-Vp64 and 8xCTS-ECFP had the cleanest OFF-state (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Combinations between the 8xCTS-ECFP reporter and dCas9-VPR or dCas9-Vp64 and the SAM system substantially improved the ON-state activation, but compromised a clean OFF-state.
source: Nevertheless, combinations between the 8xCTS-ECFP reporter and dCas9-VPR (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F) or dCas9-Vp64 and the SAM system (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G) substantially improved the ON-state activation, but compromised a clean OFF-state.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F and 1G.

claim: For first-generation designs, activation in the presence of the trigger with 100 nt 3' flank was efficient only for iSBH-sgRNA 1.
source: For first-generation designs, activation in the presence of the trigger with 100 nt 3' flank was efficient only for iSBH-sgRNA 1 (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: For second-generation iSBH-sgRNA designs, notable activation was observed for all three iSBH-sgRNAs tested with 100 nt 3' flank triggers, with ECFP production detected in 15–30% of the transfected cells.
source: For second-generation iSBH-sgRNA designs, notable activation was observed for all three iSBH-sgRNAs tested, with ECFP production detected in 15–30% of the transfected cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Second-generation iSBH-sgRNAs have superior abilities in detecting longer RNA triggers compared to first-generation designs.
source: This result confirmed that second-generation iSBH-sgRNA designs have superior abilities in detecting longer RNA triggers.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of first- and second-generation designs shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Second-generation iSBH-sgRNAs successfully detected different RNA trigger configurations, including triggers with sizes exceeding 250 nt.
source: Second-generation iSBH-sgRNAs successfully detected different RNA trigger configurations, including triggers with sizes exceeding 250 nt (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: In second-generation iSBH-sgRNAs, the requirement for complementarity between RNA trigger and the iSBH-sgRNA backfold resulted in the restriction of RNA trigger sequence choices by the spacer sequences.
source: In the second-generation iSBH-sgRNAs, the requirement for complementarity between RNA trigger and the iSBH-sgRNA backfold resulted in the restriction of RNA trigger sequence choices by the spacer sequences.
evidence: This is a description of a design constraint of second-generation iSBH-sgRNAs.

claim: Second-generation designs do not allow users to detect any RNA triggers of choice while targeting Cas9 to the desired CRISPR-targeting sequence (CTS).
source: As such, these designs do not allow users to detect any RNA triggers of choice while targeting Cas9 to the desired CRISPR-targeting sequence (CTS).
evidence: This is a description of a limitation of second-generation iSBH-sgRNAs.

claim: A modular iSBH-sgRNA prototype was conceived in which RNA triggers are only complementary to the loop and the first 15 nt of the iSBH-sgRNA backfold, and iSBH-sgRNAs have only 17 nt spacer sequences complementary with CTSs.
source: We thus conceived a modular iSBH-sgRNA prototype in which RNA triggers are only complementary to the loop and the first 15 nt of the iSBH-sgRNA backfold, and iSBH-sgRNAs have only 17 nt spacer sequences complementary with CTSs.
evidence: This is a description of the design features of modular iSBH-sgRNAs.

claim: The size of iSBH-sgRNA loops was increased to mitigate the impact of truncating RNA trigger sequences on the affinity between iSBH-sgRNAs and RNA triggers.
source: To mitigate the impact of truncating RNA trigger sequences on the affinity between iSBH-sgRNAs and RNA triggers, we increased the size of iSBH-sgRNA loops (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a description of a design strategy for modular iSBH-sgRNAs, illustrated in Figure 3A.

claim: The MODesign computational pipeline enables iSBH-sgRNA design using input RNA triggers, sgRNA spacers, and desired loop sizes.
source: Starting from the modular iSBH-sgRNA prototype, we developed the MODesign computational pipeline for enabling iSBH-sgRNA design using input RNA triggers, sgRNA spacers, and desired loop sizes (Pelea, 2025a; Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a description of the MODesign algorithm developed in this study, illustrated in Figure 3B.

claim: MODesign calculates the size of the iSBH-sgRNA trigger-sensing component and creates a list of all potential trigger sub-sequences having that particular size.
source: MODesign calculates the size of the iSBH-sgRNA trigger-sensing component and creates a list of all potential trigger sub-sequences having that particular size.
evidence: This is a description of the MODesign algorithm functionality.

claim: MODesign verifies whether resulting modular iSBH-sgRNA sequences fold into desired RNA structures using NuPACK and outputs all designs that adopt a correct fold.
source: Next, MODesign verifies whether resulting modular iSBH-sgRNA sequences fold into desired RNA structures using NuPACK (Allouche, 2011) and outputs all designs that adopt a correct fold.
evidence: This is a description of the MODesign algorithm functionality, with citation to NuPACK.

claim: Modular designs generated by the MODesign algorithm had good OFF-state activity and were activated by RNA trigger D.
source: Our results suggested that the modular designs generated by the MODesign algorithm had good OFF-state activity and were activated by RNA trigger D (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Modular iSBH-sgRNAs can be designed starting from different sgRNA spacer sequences.
source: After recognising that modular iSBH-sgRNAs can be designed starting from different sgRNA spacer sequences, a second test was performed to investigate whether these designs could detect different input triggers.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Choosing modular iSBH-sgRNAs that detect four U6-expressed triggers is possible.
source: HEK293T validation experiments showed that choosing modular iSBH-sgRNAs that detect the four U6-expressed triggers is possible (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Modular iSBH-sgRNA designs enable efficient RNA detection, especially for smaller RNAs such as triggers A and D.
source: Despite not performing quite as well as second-generation designs (Figures 2A and 3D), modular iSBH-sgRNA still enable efficient RNA detection, especially for smaller RNAs such as triggers A and D.
evidence: This is an assessment based on comparison of experimental data shown in Figures 2A and 3D.

claim: For highly efficient designs such as modular iSBH-sgRNA (D), addition of the SAM effector system boosted ON-state activation with only a negligible increase in the OFF-state non-specific activation.
source: For highly efficient designs such as modular iSBH-sgRNA (D), addition of the SAM effector system (Konermann et al., 2015) boosted ON-state activation with only a negligible increase in the OFF-state non-specific activation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Activation of modular iSBH-sgRNA designs was specifically conditioned by complementary RNA triggers.
source: Orthogonality tests suggested that activation of modular iSBH-sgRNA designs was specifically conditioned by complementary RNA triggers (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 2), showing the exquisite specificity of the system.
evidence: This is supported by orthogonality test data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: In eukaryotic cells double-stranded RNAs are recognised and cleaved by endogenous RNA processing pathways such as RNA interference (RNAi).
source: It is known that in eukaryotic cells double-stranded RNAs are recognised and cleaved by endogenous RNA processing pathways such as RNA interference (RNAi, Meister and Tuschl, 2004; Pong and Gullerova, 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The interaction between iSBH-sgRNAs and RNA triggers leads to the formation of long double-stranded RNA structures.
source: Furthermore, the interaction between iSBH-sgRNAs and RNA triggers leads to the formation of long double-stranded RNA structures and similar structures were reported to act as a non-canonical substrate for Dicer (Pong and Gullerova, 2018; Burger et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference based on the design of iSBH-sgRNAs and cited literature.

claim: Long double-stranded RNA structures similar to those formed by iSBH-sgRNAs and RNA triggers were reported to act as a non-canonical substrate for Dicer.
source: Furthermore, the interaction between iSBH-sgRNAs and RNA triggers leads to the formation of long double-stranded RNA structures and similar structures were reported to act as a non-canonical substrate for Dicer (Pong and Gullerova, 2018; Burger et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: In the absence of RNA triggers, recovered iSBH-sgRNA RT-PCR bands matched the expected 137 bp size.
source: In the absence of RNA triggers, recovered iSBH-sgRNA RT-PCR bands matched the expected 137 bp size.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: In the presence of dCas9-Vp64 and complementary RNA triggers, the iSBH-sgRNA band sizes decreased to 81 bp, similar to bands recovered from non-engineered native sgRNA control.
source: In the presence of dCas9-Vp64 and complementary RNA triggers, the band sizes decreased to 81 bp, similar to bands recovered from non-engineered native sgRNA control.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Engineered sgRNA components (extension, loop, backfold) were removed from iSBH-sgRNAs during activation.
source: These results suggested that engineered sgRNA components (extension, loop, backfold) were removed from iSBH-sgRNAs during activation, and this hypothesis was confirmed by sequencing PCR products recovered from truncated samples (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and sequencing data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In the absence of dCas9-Vp64, out of 3 iSBH-sgRNAs tested, only iSBH-sgRNA 1 gets efficiently truncated.
source: In the absence of dCas9-Vp64, out of 3 iSBH-sgRNAs tested, only iSBH-sgRNA 1 gets efficiently truncated (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The formation of sgRNAs with 20 nt spacers may be dCas9-dependent.
source: These results suggested that the formation of sgRNAs with 20 nt spacers may be dCas9-dependent.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data shown in Figure 4B and 4C.

claim: When RNA triggers were present, the conformational change enabled iSBH-sgRNAs to bind to dCas9, leading to iSBH-sgRNA truncation.
source: However, when RNA triggers were present, the conformational change enabled iSBH-sgRNAs to bind to dCas9, leading to iSBH-sgRNA truncation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Engineered sgRNAs with extended spacer sequences are processed to original 20 nt spacer lengths.
source: These results are also supported by previous studies reporting that engineered sgRNAs with extended spacer sequences are processed to original 20 nt spacer lengths (Perli et al., 2016; Ran et al., 2013a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: RNA triggers are truncated specifically in the presence of matching iSBH-sgRNAs.
source: The results demonstrated that RNA triggers are truncated specifically in the presence of matching iSBH-sgRNAs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: When co-transfected together with iSBH-sgRNAs with incompatible hairpins, RNA triggers remained intact.
source: When co-transfected together with iSBH-sgRNAs with incompatible hairpins, RNA triggers remained intact.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Truncation of RNA triggers was not dCas9-dependent.
source: Interestingly, unlike iSBH-sgRNAs, truncation of RNA triggers was not dCas9-dependent (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Sequencing results confirmed deletions in the truncated RNA triggers that overlapped with the 44 nt sequence complementary with iSBH-sgRNAs.
source: Sequencing results confirmed deletions in the truncated RNA triggers that overlapped with the 44 nt sequence complementary with iSBH-sgRNAs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: RNA circularisation assays suggested the involvement of double-stranded RNA processing mechanisms when iSBH-sgRNAs are deployed.
source: To sum up, RNA circularisation assays suggested the involvement of double-stranded RNA processing mechanisms when iSBH-sgRNAs are deployed.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: dCas9 seems involved in truncating iSBH-sgRNA sequences in the presence of complementary RNA triggers.
source: Interestingly, dCas9 also seems involved in truncating iSBH-sgRNA sequences in the presence of complementary RNA triggers.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Two transgenic zebrafish lines encoding dCas9-Vp64 and the 8xCTS-ECFP reporter were generated.
source: We generated two transgenic zebrafish lines encoding dCas9-Vp64 and the 8xCTS-ECFP reporter recognised by one of our best-performing sgRNAs tested in mammalian cells (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental approach, illustrated in Figure 5A.

claim: Injection of native sgRNAs with chemical modifications resulted in optimal ECFP activation across tissues in transgenic zebrafish embryos.
source: After multiple optimisation steps, injection of native sgRNAs with chemical modifications resulted in optimal ECFP activation across tissues.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: ECFP activation persisted several days post-injection of native sgRNAs in transgenic zebrafish embryos.
source: Furthermore, ECFP activation persisted several days post-injection (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: A first iteration of chemically modified iSBH-sgRNAs designed to protect the 5' end of the iSBH-sgRNA and the sgRNA scaffold did not lead to activation of the 8xCTS-ECFP reporter when co-injected with chemically synthesised RNA triggers.
source: However, when co-injected with chemically synthesised RNA triggers, these modifications did not lead to activation of the 8xCTS-ECFP reporter (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: In a first iteration of chemically modified iSBH-sgRNAs, truncation would lead to a production of sgRNAs with unprotected spacer sequences.
source: Our mechanistic data suggested that iSBH-sgRNAs get truncated during activation (Figure 4) and, in a first iteration of chemically modified iSBH-sgRNAs, such truncation would lead to a production of sgRNAs with unprotected spacer sequences.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mechanistic data shown in Figure 4 and the design of the first iteration of chemical modifications.

claim: 5'–3' sgRNA degradation was likely to occur in the first iteration of chemically modified iSBH-sgRNAs.
source: In this scenario, 5'–3' sgRNA degradation was likely to occur.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mechanistic understanding and the design of the first iteration of chemical modifications.

claim: Additional chemical modifications in the spacer sequence would reduce degradation by cellular nucleases and promote iSBH-sgRNA function in vivo.
source: We thus reasoned that additional chemical modifications in the spacer sequence would reduce degradation by cellular nucleases and promote iSBH-sgRNA function in vivo.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the mechanistic understanding and the design of the second iteration of chemical modifications.

claim: iSBH-sgRNAs synthesised using the second chemical modification strategy were injected in the absence or presence of chemically synthesised RNA triggers, and stronger ECFP signals were detected in the presence of matching RNA triggers.
source: iSBH-sgRNAs synthesised using our second chemical modification strategy (Figure 5C) were injected in the absence or presence of chemically synthesised RNA triggers (Figure 5B), and stronger ECFP signals were detected in the presence of matching RNA triggers (iSBH-sgRNA ON, Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: χ2 tests performed for three experimental replicates showed that the presence of RNA triggers causes a statistically significant change in ECFP expression in zebrafish embryos.
source: χ2 tests (Figure 5E) performed for three experimental replicates showed that the presence of RNA triggers causes a statistically significant change in ECFP expression.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: In contrast with the iSBH-sgRNA (OFF) condition, the iSBH-sgRNA (ON) condition presented an average of 3.2-fold increase in the number of embryos with high ECFP signals.
source: In contrast with the iSBH-sgRNA (OFF) condition, the iSBH-sgRNA (ON) condition presented an average of 3.2-fold increase in the number of embryos with high ECFP signals.
evidence: This is supported by quantification of experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The average number of embryos with no ECFP signals recovered in the iSBH-sgRNA (ON) condition was lower than in the iSBH-sgRNA (OFF) condition.
source: Furthermore, the average number of embryos with no ECFP signals recovered in the iSBH-sgRNA (ON) condition was lower than in the iSBH-sgRNA (OFF) condition.
evidence: This is supported by quantification of experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: iSBH-sgRNAs are functional in developing zebrafish embryos.
source: Our results show that iSBH-sgRNAs are functional in developing zebrafish embryos.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Gaining insight into the mechanism of the iSBH-sgRNA activation has allowed identification of critical positions for chemical modifications that stabilised the design.
source: Furthermore, gaining insight into the mechanism of the iSBH-sgRNA activation has allowed us to identify critical positions for chemical modifications that stabilised our design.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the mechanistic studies and the successful application of chemical modifications in zebrafish.

claim: The choice of CRISPR activators and reporters greatly influences the dynamic ranges of iSBH-sgRNA activation.
source: Our data show that the choice of CRISPR activators and reporters greatly influences the dynamic ranges of iSBH-sgRNA activation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the comparison of different CRISPRa systems shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: dCas9 is involved in iSBH-sgRNA processing and activation.
source: Our results suggest that dCas9 is involved in iSBH-sgRNA processing and activation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the mechanistic data shown in Figure 4.

claim: iSBH-sgRNA truncation to sgRNA sequences that have 20 nt spacers is consistent with previous observations reported in studies that attempt to extend spacer sequences.
source: iSBH-sgRNA truncation to sgRNA sequences that have 20 nt spacers is consistent with previous observations reported in studies that attempt to extend spacer sequences (Perli et al., 2016; Ran et al., 2013a).
evidence: This is a comparison of the current findings with published literature.

claim: RNA triggers are cleaved by endogenous factors and molecules from the RNA interference pathway could be responsible for the cleavage.
source: Our data suggest that RNA triggers are cleaved by endogenous factors and molecules from the RNA interference pathway (Meister and Tuschl, 2004; Pong and Gullerova, 2018) could be responsible for the cleavage.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data shown in Figure 4 and cited literature.

claim: To date, a variety of RNA-inducible gRNA designs have been developed.
source: To date, a variety of RNA-inducible gRNA designs have been developed (Hanewich-Hollatz et al., 2019; Hochrein et al., 2021; Jakimo et al., 2018; Jiao et al., 2021; Jin et al., 2019; Li et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2022; Lin et al., 2020; Siu and Chen, 2019; Galizi et al., 2020; Hunt and Chen, 2022a; Hunt and Chen, 2022b; Ying et al., 2020; Choi et al., 2023).
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field supported by multiple citations.

claim: There is a lack of direct, head-to-head comparisons of RNA-inducible gRNA designs under standardised experimental conditions.
source: Nevertheless, there is a lack of direct, head-to-head comparisons of these designs under standardised experimental conditions.
evidence: This is an assessment of the state of the field.

claim: It is challenging to conclusively determine which RNA-inducible gRNA design exhibits superior properties.
source: Consequently, it is challenging to conclusively determine which design exhibits superior properties (Pelea et al., 2022).
evidence: This is an assessment of the state of the field supported by citation.

claim: To the best of our knowledge, the iSBH-sgRNA system is the first RNA-inducible gRNA design tested in vivo.
source: Notably, to the best of our knowledge, the iSBH-sgRNA system is the first RNA-inducible gRNA design tested in vivo and characterising the iSBH-sgRNA activation mechanism was essential for implementing iSBH-sgRNA technology in zebrafish embryos.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the work based on the authors' knowledge of the field.

claim: Characterising the iSBH-sgRNA activation mechanism was essential for implementing iSBH-sgRNA technology in zebrafish embryos.
